newsitem.title: KENYA: Pro-reform Kenya alliance accuses Moi of division.
newsitem.headline: Pro-reform Kenya alliance accuses Moi of division.

text.p: An opposition-backed alliance pressing for constitutional reforms in Kenya accused President Daniel arap Moi on Monday of seeking to divide their movement.

National Convention Executive Council (NCEC) official Kivutha Kibwana told a news conference Moi's government was about to hold talks on reforms with a group of parliamentarians but "without the widest consultion among all concerned".
Kibwana said political parties were not representative enough for a dialogue and could not speak for the NCEC, which provided what he called the framework for dialogue on reforms.

The NCEC is a coalition of political parties, human rights bodies, civic groups and churches that had united Kenya's squabbling political parties in a rare show of unity in demanding reforms before presidential and parliamentary polls.
But that unity is sorely tested by Moi's agreeing to meet opposition parties this week and by the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party agreeing to some reforms last week.
Michael Wamalwa, the leader of the opposition in parliament, was expected to discuss reforms with the president on Tuesday.
No date has been set for this year's general election but some opposition parties fear Moi wants to call it shortly after bills are approved by parliament, where KANU has a majority.
"All dialogue with the KANU government pertaining to the issue of constitutional reforms before the general election must be conducted within the auspicies of the NCEC," Kibwana said.

"Attempts by President Moi to talk to groups of individuals not representative of the broad spectrum will not work. That is trying to subvert the interest of Kenyans and that will not break their determination for genuine change," Kibwana added.

Monday's news conference was also attended by opposition party leader Raila Odinga, opposition politicians, Kenya's former wildlife guardian Richard Leakey and leading dissidents Koigi wa Wamwere and Sheikh Khalid Balala.
At least nine people were killed in Kenya on July 7 during a day of police breaking up demonstrations called by the NCEC,
Following the worst political unrest in Kenya in seven years, KANU which is led by Moi, offered its package of reforms and a constitutional review, which would end after the polls.
Attorney-General Amos Wako said on Friday he had began work on draft legislation which would be ready in two weeks.
One bill would give the president powers to appoint a commission to review the entire constitution, he said.
The second would repeal or ammend 11 laws the opposition says are oppressive. The bills would be presented to the cabinet for approval before being tabled in parliament, Wako said.
NCEC member Gibson Kamau Kuria said such a move by Wako was wrong because a final reform package sent to parliament had to be negotiated and agreed between the NCEC and the government.
Students from the University of Nairobi and Jomo Kenyatta University closed two weeks ago following clashes with riot police over constitutional reforms trickled back on Monday.
Final year students at the two universities reported back and other students were called for staggered returns over the next week. The two universities had a total of 25,000 students.
Kibwana said NCEC protests planned for the rest of July and August will go ahead, starting with a day of prayer in Kenya's Indian Ocean port of Mombasa on Friday and a rally on Saturday.
Mombasa, Kenya's second city, is the coast centre of its tourism industry, the country's main foreign exchange earner.
